paper_metadata.title: Tertiary dendritic instability in late stage solidification of Ni-based superalloys
paper_metadata.journal: Modelling and Simulation in Materials Science and Engineering

evidence.quote: Ni-based superalloys with high segregation levels show significant instability in secondary dendrite arms and an increased tendency for tertiary arm formation, respectively.

The compositions of the investigated alloys represent derivatives of the commercial Ni-based superalloy CMSX-4 with changes in the Al, Ta, Ti and Hf content, as well as the complete removal of Re (table 1).
The melt was homogenized for 5 min at 1560 °C before casting into the 1500 °C preheated mould (figure 1).

In particular, no tertiary arm formation is observed for alloy1 (figure 2(a)), while alloy3 displays some tertiary branching (figure 2(b)). Alloy5 is characterized by very significant tertiary arm formation (figure 2(c)), i.e. pronounced instabilities of secondary dendrite arms with respect to alloy1, where the secondary arms show an almost convex contour.

In general, a large solidification range corresponds to a large amount of solute to be redistributed at the growing interface. This leads to the so-called growth restriction, which has to be overcome by a fine microstructure.
Highly segregating elements such as Ta and Hf enlarge the concentration gradient Δc and impede the redistribution process at the growing interface during solidification.

Alloys that are characterized by high segregation levels display large values of ΔTint and an increased tendency for tertiary arm formation.

Highly segregating elements such as Ta and Hf enlarge the concentration gradient Δc and impede the redistribution process at the growing interface during solidification. This leads to the so-called growth restriction that provides a refined microstructure at the end of solidification
